diff_user.system: You are optimizing a Go function. Popcount(xs []uint64) int must return the total number of set bits across all words of xs. Each candidate is scored by running it in giri, a Go SSA interpreter, on 50 test vectors. It must return the reference result on every vector, and leave xs unchanged. Among correct candidates, a lower abstract cost (the number of SSA instructions executed over all vectors) scores higher, and any correct candidate scores above any incorrect one. The only import allowed is math/bits. Keep the function's name and signature.
responses:
## Analysis

The current program is a fully unrolled binary ladder with a recursive peel of 16 words. Its abstract cost is 3567 against a reference cost of 7570, and every attempt so far has landed on exactly 3567. The earlier edits only reshuffled control flow, which the SSA pipeline likely normalizes away, so they produced identical costs.

The remaining per-word overhead is in bounds checks. Each `xs[i]` with a non-constant slice length emits its own `IsInBounds` check plus an index computation. In the 16-word peel, that is 16 checks per call. Reslicing once to a fixed-length array view, `y := xs[:16]`, lets the compiler prove every `y[i]` (with `i < 16`) is in range after a single check on the reslice. That should remove roughly 15 bounds-check instructions per 16-word block, which is the largest remaining per-word cost I can see.

The same idea applies to the 8-word block, and to the 4-word block. I'm limiting the change to the 16-word peel, since it is the hot path for large inputs. Behavior is unchanged: the same words are summed, `xs` is not modified, and the recursion is the same.

## Expected effect

- Fewer `IsInBounds` checks and index computations on the 16-word hot path, so the abstract cost should drop below 3567 for inputs with length of at least 16.
- Inputs shorter than 16 are unaffected, so correctness holds on all vectors.
- If the cost does not move, the test vectors are probably dominated by short slices, and the next step would be to apply the same reslice trick to the 8- and 4-word blocks.
